title: Token anatomy bench: the same text, several-fold different token counts

groups.label: Long Chinese sentence
groups.text: 明天北京适合野餐吗？记得带上防晒霜。
groups.note: Chinese is often segmented at 1–2 characters per token, with no direct equivalent of a word boundary.

groups.label: English sentence
groups.text: The weather looks perfect for a picnic tomorrow morning.
groups.note: Frequent English words tend to be one token each; longer words get split into subword pieces.

groups.label: Mixed Chinese–English
groups.text: 把 request timeout 调到 30s 再重试。
groups.note: Script-switch boundaries tend to produce isolated single-character tokens, so mixed-script text is often under-budgeted.

groups.label: Code snippet
groups.note: Identifiers, indentation, and punctuation each become tokens; code has a much higher token density than natural language.

groups.label: Emoji & symbols
groups.note: One emoji often costs 2–3 tokens — the lightest character on screen, the heaviest on the bill.

groups.label: Numbers & order IDs
groups.note: Long digit runs get split segment by segment; to save tokens, never feed program-generated order IDs to the model.
